analysis.one_liner: Caps malpractice awards for pain and suffering at $250,000 and restricts health care lawsuits, while ending health insurers' antitrust exemption.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 223-181 on March 22, 2012, with 216 of 241 voting Republicans in favor and 171 of 190 voting Democrats opposed; the Senate never voted, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the rules for lawsuits over medical injuries nationwide. It would cap compensation for pain and suffering at $250,000 no matter how bad the injury, cap lawyers' contingency fees, shorten the time to sue, and make it nearly impossible to win punitive damages against a drug or device that the FDA approved. It would also strip health insurers of their long-standing exemption from antitrust laws, limit liability for emergency-room care, and repeal a board created by the health law to propose Medicare cuts.
analysis.who_benefits: Physicians, hospitals, nursing homes, and medical malpractice insurers gain the most: caps and fee limits directly cut the amounts they must pay injured patients and shrink the number of lawsuits worth bringing. Drug and device makers gain a shield from punitive damages whenever their product followed FDA rules. Consumers also gain one real win: health insurers would lose their antitrust exemption, exposing practices like price fixing to competition law. Volunteer health professionals responding to disasters would be shielded from lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Doctors, hospitals, malpractice insurers, drug makers

how_it_helps.text: Caps compensation for noneconomic harms like pain and suffering at $250,000 per case, while leaving payment for actual financial losses such as medical bills and lost wages unlimited.
Caps lawyers' contingency fees on a sliding scale, from 40% of the first $50,000 down to 15% of anything above $600,000, and lets courts redirect fees they consider excessive.

Bars punitive damages against manufacturers of drugs or devices that were approved, cleared, or licensed by the FDA, unless the company hid required information from the FDA, bribed an FDA official, or sold an adulterated or misbranded product.
Replaces joint liability with proportional fault, so each defendant pays only its own share of an award rather than covering the share of others who cannot pay.

Strips health insurers of their exemption from federal antitrust laws under the McCarran-Ferguson Act, so anticompetitive conduct in health insurance can be challenged — though it also bars most private antitrust class actions against insurers.

Deems emergency-room physicians and hospitals to be employees of the Public Health Service, which limits their liability for care required under the emergency-treatment law, and shields volunteer health professionals from lawsuits during federally declared disasters.

analysis.who_pays: Patients catastrophically injured by medical negligence, and families of patients who died. A child or a retiree who suffers lifelong harm typically has small wage losses, so the $250,000 cap on pain and suffering covers most of what they can recover — the same amount for a minor injury or a lifetime of disability. Fee caps can make it uneconomical for lawyers to take smaller injury cases at all, so some genuinely injured patients would recover nothing. Plaintiffs' trial lawyers bear the direct financial cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Injured patients and plaintiffs' trial lawyers

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 cap on pain-and-suffering damages applies regardless of how severe the injury is, and is the same whether the victim is a wage earner or a child or retiree with little earnings to count as economic damages — so the cap hits exactly the patients least able to prove financial loss.

Contingency-fee caps reduce what lawyers can earn on a case, which can make it uneconomical to bring smaller but legitimate injury claims — meaning some patients with real injuries would get no recovery at all, since malpractice cases are almost always taken on contingency.

Punitive damages would be essentially unavailable against drug and device manufacturers whose products met FDA standards, removing the strongest financial deterrent for a company that knew of a safety problem the FDA had not yet acted on.
Juries would be allowed to hear that the victim's injuries were already paid for by health insurance, which can reduce awards below what patients actually lost out of pocket.

The antitrust title applies only to health insurance and simultaneously forbids private class actions against insurers for antitrust violations, reserving enforcement mainly to the government and states.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a genuine trade rather than a one-sided giveaway, but the trade falls hardest on a small group: patients with the worst injuries and the smallest paychecks. Supporters argued that capping malpractice awards would lower malpractice insurance premiums and reduce defensive medicine, slightly lowering everyone's health costs — that claim was the core of the case for the bill, and it was contested. The consumer-side gains are real but partial: the antitrust title ends insurers' competition exemption yet blocks most private class actions, and the emergency-care and disaster-volunteer protections are modest. Weighed honestly, the bill's central and largest effect is to cut what injured patients and their lawyers can recover, with the promised savings to the broader public uncertain; the antitrust provision is the one clear, unambiguous win for ordinary consumers.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed the bill on a mostly party-line vote, but the Democratic-led Senate left it on its calendar without ever scheduling a vote, and it died when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 24, 2011, and reported from both the Judiciary Committee (18-15) and the Energy and Commerce Committee (30-20) by May 2011.
The House passed the bill 223-181 on March 22, 2012, with 216 of 241 voting Republicans in favor, 10 Republicans opposed, 7 of 190 voting Democrats in favor, and 171 opposed.
A Democratic motion to send the bill back with instructions to protect Medicare benefits failed 180-229, with 228 of 241 voting Republicans against it.
The bill was read twice in the Senate and placed on the Senate calendar in March and April 2012 but was never debated or voted on, and expired at the end of the 112th Congress in January 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, injured patients kept their full rights to jury awards under state law, and malpractice insurers, hospitals, and drug and device makers kept facing uncapped state-law liability. Health insurers also kept their antitrust exemption — the one part of the bill that worked against them never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured patients and malpractice insurers' adversaries

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split almost entirely by party: Republicans voted 216-10 in favor, Democrats 7-171 against; a bipartisan exception was the bill's antitrust title, which had Democratic roots.

industries.note: The damage caps, fee limits, and shorter filing deadlines directly cut both the size and the number of claims these insurers must pay. Their gain comes dollar-for-dollar out of what injured patients can recover.

The bill cuts their malpractice exposure and deems emergency-room providers to be federal employees with limited liability. Providers argued lower insurance costs would slow health spending and keep doctors practicing; patients' compensation is the offsetting cost.

The bill bars punitive damages against makers of FDA-approved products and limits each defendant to its proportional share of fault. Compliance with FDA approval becomes a nearly complete shield, even when a company knew of harms the FDA had not addressed.

Fee caps on a sliding scale and the $250,000 damages cap shrink the value of most malpractice cases, which would push many injury claims out of the market entirely. Their financial interest runs with their clients' ability to recover.

The bill strips health insurers of their McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption, exposing price-fixing and market allocation to antitrust law, but it also blocks most private antitrust class actions against them, limiting enforcement mainly to government plaintiffs.
